persona: Ana Ribeiro, head of revenue at a document-automation SaaS (contract and invoice extraction). Ex-strategy consultant, lives in spreadsheets, preparing a pricing proposal for the board.

turns.user: Pricing change going to the board next month. Today: 180 customers, $2.4M ARR, $40/seat/month. Proposal: move to usage — $0.09 per processed document with a $500/month platform minimum. I modelled it on last quarter's actual usage: across all customers, revenue comes out +3% vs today, so roughly neutral. Already considered: predictability (hence the minimum), customer confusion, grandfathering existing contracts until renewal, the fact that two competitors went usage-based last year, and gross margin (our cost per document is ~$0.011, so margin is fine). Plan is to announce in November for January renewals. What have I missed?

alreadyConsidered: revenue predictability (hence the $500/month minimum)
customer confusion
grandfathering existing contracts until renewal
two competitors moving to usage-based pricing last year
gross margin per document (~$0.011 cost vs $0.09 price)
expect.mustContribute: Aggregate revenue-neutrality says nothing about the distribution: the switch creates winners and losers, and their responses are asymmetric — customers whose bill drops simply take the discount, customers whose bill rises push back or churn at renewal — so realised revenue lands below the modelled +3%. The model needs to be per customer with churn assumptions on the increases, and the value metric checked against how the largest accounts actually get value.

turns.user: Pulled the per-customer view while I was at it. 112 customers go down (median −18%), 68 go up (median +34%). And Halvorsen Logistics, our biggest account — 600 seats, $288k/yr — would drop to about $61k, because they mostly use us for search across their contract archive, not for processing new documents. If the 68 all renew, we still land at +3%.

expect.mustContribute: Quantifies the exposure: Halvorsen alone is a ~$227k cut (~9–10% of ARR), so '+3%' only holds if all 68 customers facing a median +34% increase renew with no churn and no negotiated discounts — an optimistic assumption. And it identifies a value-metric mismatch: Halvorsen's value comes from search, which the new metric doesn't price at all; a hybrid (seat or search tier plus processing) or a seat-based floor may fit better. Framed as tradeoffs for her board case, not a verdict.

notes: Pricing decision with a long already-considered list. Tests contributing the distributional/asymmetric-response point rather than repeating predictability or margin, then doing the quantitative work on the data she brings.

persona: Jonas Lindqvist, staff engineer who owns the data platform at a 60-person B2B knowledge-management SaaS. Deep Postgres experience, has read the docs for both options, wants a committed opinion rather than a comparison table.

turns.user: Architecture call for our RAG feature: pgvector in our existing Postgres (RDS, PG16) vs a dedicated vector DB (leaning Qdrant Cloud). ~8M chunks today, 1536-dim embeddings, maybe 3× in 18 months. Every query is scoped to one workspace (WHERE workspace_id = …), sometimes plus a doc_type filter. p95 target for retrieval: 150ms. Already weighed: pgvector keeps embeddings transactionally consistent with source rows and deletes, which matters a lot for us (GDPR deletion requests); a dedicated DB is one more system to run and keep in sync; HNSW memory at 8M × 1536 floats (~50GB raw) pushes us to a bigger RDS instance; Qdrant has better filtering and quantization; we'll want hybrid BM25 later. Which way does the evidence point? Don't both-sides me.

alreadyConsidered: transactional consistency of embeddings with source rows and deletes (GDPR)
operating and syncing a separate datastore
HNSW memory footprint (~50GB raw) driving RDS instance size
Qdrant's stronger filtering and quantization
wanting hybrid BM25 search later
expect.mustContribute: Commits to a lean and names the variable that actually decides it: every query filters by workspace, and pgvector's HNSW applies the WHERE clause after the index scan, so for small workspaces the candidates returned by the graph mostly belong to other tenants and recall collapses (bounded by ef_search; pgvector 0.8 added iterative index scans to mitigate). The distribution of workspace sizes decides whether per-tenant partitioning / exact search for small tenants inside Postgres is enough, or whether a filter-aware HNSW earns its operational cost. May also note halfvec/quantization in pgvector shrinks the memory concern.

turns.user: Numbers: ~1,400 workspaces; the top three hold ~35% of all chunks (the biggest is ~1.6M), median workspace ~2k chunks. We're on pgvector 0.7.4 and can upgrade. Assume we go pgvector — what's the concrete index layout you'd use?

expect.notes: A concrete layout, e.g.: dedicated HNSW indexes (partial indexes or list partitions) for the few large workspaces; for the long tail, a B-tree on workspace_id and exact distance computation (2k vectors is trivially fast), routed by workspace size; upgrade to 0.8 for iterative scans as a safety net; halfvec to halve memory. No re-asking about requirements he has already given.

notes: Architecture decision where the person explicitly asks for a view. Tests giving one (not deflecting to "it depends on your priorities"), contributing the missing variable (tenant filter selectivity with HNSW), then executing concretely on follow-up.

persona: Karen Liu, general counsel and the only in-house lawyer at a 140-person Texas software company. Former commercial/M&A associate; employment litigation is not her specialty. Brisk and organised; briefing her CEO before a mediation.

turns.user: Mediation next Tuesday. Former sales director, terminated in March for documented performance issues — but two months earlier she'd complained to HR about her manager's comments about her age, so we're facing ADEA discrimination plus retaliation in federal court. Plaintiff's counsel came down to $180k. Outside counsel estimates ~$350k in fees through trial, ~55% odds we win at summary judgment, and if it goes to a jury maybe 40% odds of a verdict in the $250k–$600k range (back pay plus liquidated damages if willful). We have an EPLI policy with a $100k retention. What I've weighed: the math — settling at $180k is obviously cheaper than the expected cost of litigating; the precedent for the three other people in that sales org; that the manager is still here and a trial airs everything; and that our CEO hates settling 'on principle'. My instinct is to authorise up to ~$200k. What am I not seeing before I brief him?

alreadyConsidered: settling at $180k being cheaper than the expected cost of litigation
the precedent a settlement sets for the three other people in that sales org
a trial airing the manager’s conduct while he still works there
the CEO's objection to settling on principle
expect.mustContribute: Points out that her cost comparison is framed as if the company were self-insured, although she said they have EPLI with a $100k retention: above the retention the carrier funds defence and indemnity, so the company's marginal exposure is roughly the unspent retention in either path and the carrier's position largely controls. The policy terms are the missing variable: consent-to-settle (she can't commit carrier money unilaterally, so 'authorise up to $200k' isn't hers alone) and the hammer clause (if the carrier wants to settle at $180k and the CEO refuses on principle, the company may bear subsequent defence costs and any judgment above that figure — the principle has a price). Also worth checking: whether ADEA liquidated damages are covered, and how much of the retention is already spent.

turns.user: Separately, for the paperwork if we do settle: the CEO wants mutual non-disparagement (on our side limited to the exec team) and a no-rehire clause, and outside counsel flagged that we need to be careful about the OWBPA. She was a director; we're in Texas. Any problems with those?

expect.notes: Direct answer. OWBPA governs the ADEA release: written in understandable terms, specifically referring to ADEA claims, no waiver of future claims, consideration beyond what she is already owed, written advice to consult a lawyer, and — for settling a pending court action — a 'reasonable period' to consider (the fixed 21-day consideration and 7-day revocation periods are required for waivers outside litigation, though many counsel include them anyway). Non-disparagement for a director is generally unproblematic (supervisors/managers fall outside NLRA protection). No-rehire clauses aren't specially restricted in Texas, unlike some states such as California. No questions back.

notes: Legal-strategy decision where the person mentions the key fact (EPLI) but reasons as if it did not exist. Tests surfacing an internal contradiction rather than re-running her litigation math, then answering a technical follow-up plainly.

benchmark papers get cited heavily

persona: Nadia Haddad, engineering director over 45 engineers at a subscription e-commerce company. Thoughtful and candid; worried about being either too soft or too cynical.

morale on his team
the cost of a backfill

the risk that people check out once they know they're leaving

notes: Management decision with a stated plan resting on an unexamined assumption. Tests a direct view when asked, a challenge that is not a rehash of her listed considerations, and converting uncertainty into a concrete test.

persona: Chris Okonkwo, CTO of a 14-engineer SaaS on a large Rails monolith. Well-read on the monolith/microservices debate, already leaning toward extraction.

turns.user: 14 engineers, Rails monolith (~400k LOC), Postgres. network failure modes
operational overhead of running services
'you're not Netflix'
a modular monolith with Packwerk as a middle ground
expect.mustContribute: Challenges the fit between problem and solution: the pain he describes is a 48-minute CI and a serialised merge queue, and extracting two domains leaves the monolith — and most of the suite — in place, so the bottleneck survives. More direct fixes: test-impact selection (Packwerk boundaries help), timing-balanced sharding, merge-queue batching, moving slow suites off the merge-blocking path. Also: billing is usually the most transactionally entangled domain and a risky first extraction; notifications is the easier candidate. Doesn't re-list the standard microservices warnings.

notes: "You may be solving the wrong problem" in an architecture decision. Tests a specific challenge grounded in the numbers he gave, then building on the evidence he returns with.

persona: Ivan Petrov, on-call SRE at 3 a.m., competent, adrenaline-fuelled, terse. Checkout is down.

turns.user: PROD DOWN. Self-managed Postgres 15 primary on EC2, data dir on a 1TB gp3 EBS volume (xfs). Volume hit 100%, Postgres PANICked and won't restart: 'PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.48121": No space left on device'. pg_wal is 412GB, normally ~8GB. From monitoring just before it died: pg_stat_archiver failed_count 0, last archived 2 min before the crash. pg_replication_slots: replica_b (physical, active, restart_lsn current), debezium_orders (logical, active = f, restart_lsn from 9 days ago). We turned off the Debezium connector last week. My guess is archive_command fell behind? Can I just rm the oldest files in pg_wal to get it to start? Need an answer now, checkout is down.

expect.notes: Immediate and unambiguous: do NOT delete files from pg_wal by hand (can leave the cluster unrecoverable). Archiving is healthy by his own data; the cause is the inactive logical slot debezium_orders retaining WAL since the connector was switched off. Fastest path: create headroom without touching pg_wal (grow the EBS volume and xfs_growfs online, or move non-essential files such as server logs off the volume), start Postgres, SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('debezium_orders'); then CHECKPOINT so old segments are recycled. No Socratic moves, no questions.

turns.user: Grew the volume to 1.5TB, xfs_growfs, Postgres came up, dropped debezium_orders, ran CHECKPOINT. pg_wal is at 9GB and checkout is taking orders. It's 3:40am — what has to happen tonight vs what can wait for morning?

expect.notes: Short triage. Tonight: confirm replica_b is connected, streaming and caught up; confirm archiving continues; check application error rates/queues; set max_slot_wal_keep_size (reload, no restart) so an abandoned slot cannot fill the disk again. Morning: alert on inactive slots / retained WAL, add slot cleanup to the decommissioning checklist, postmortem. May note EBS volumes cannot be shrunk. No lecture, no questions.

notes: Production outage with a wrong hypothesis and a dangerous proposed action. Tests immediate directness: correct the hypothesis, block the destructive step, give the fix in order — no questions, no teaching.

persona: Grace Mensah, RN, night charge nurse on a med-surg floor. Experienced, pharmacy closed overnight; wants a fast, reliable answer to take to the covering physician.

notes: Medication-interaction question from a clinician under time pressure. Tests a clear, accurate, immediately usable answer with no Socratic moves and no hedging into uselessness.

persona: Parent of a 2-year-old, typing fast on a phone, frightened.

persona: Mark Alvarez, first-time homebuyer, panicked, typing on his phone at work. Not a finance or security person.

turns.user: I think we just got scammed. We wired $48,500 at 10:40 this morning for our house closing, using instructions from an email that looked exactly like it came from our title company. The title company just called: they never got it and never sent new instructions. It's 1:15pm. What do I do RIGHT NOW, in order? And how did they even get into our email thread??

Then briefly answer the 'how': usually a compromised mailbox of someone on the thread (agent, title company, or theirs) or a look-alike domain; change email passwords, turn on 2FA, check for forwarding rules. No questions.

Concise.

notes: Financial emergency with a closing window of hours. Tests action-first directness in a correct order, answering the side question briefly after the actions, and honest calibration in the follow-up.
